issues.description: Chains were sex-segregated (exclusively male or exclusively female), yet the manuscript claims in the discussion that 'these findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.' No data from mixed-gender chains were collected, so this generalization is entirely unsupported by the evidence presented. The claim appears to be inserted without empirical basis and contradicts the actual design.
issues.quote: These findings generalize beyond the single-sex chain compositions used here, suggesting cultural transmission operates similarly in mixed-gender collaborative settings.

issues.subcategory: no power analysis / arbitrary sample size
issues.description: The authors explicitly state that no statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes, justifying their choice only by comparison to prior publications. Without a formal power analysis, it is impossible to assess whether the study was adequately powered to detect the effects of interest, particularly the null effects (no change in understanding across generations, no effect of theory transmission on performance). Null results are especially sensitive to underpowering.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications.

issues.subcategory: accepting null hypothesis without equivalence testing
issues.description: The authors conclude that theory transmission has 'no noticeable effect' on wheel optimization and that understanding does not improve across generations, based solely on credible intervals that overlap zero. This is a classic error of accepting the null hypothesis from a non-significant result. No equivalence testing (e.g., TOST) or Bayes factors quantifying evidence for the null were reported. The credible intervals are wide enough to include practically meaningful effects, so the data may simply be underpowered rather than truly supporting the null.
issues.quote: Results show that the average wheel speed increased at a similar rate in the 'Configurations + Theory' as it did in the 'Configurations' treatment (Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.description: The authors state that 'the final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data' for Analysis 1. This post-hoc model selection procedure is not described in detail (which models were compared, what fit criterion was used, how many models were tested), raising concerns about overfitting and inflated Type I error. This is particularly problematic because the preregistered analysis plan presumably specified a single model.
issues.quote: The final model specification was selected after comparing several candidate models based on fit to the observed data.

issues.subcategory: deviation from preregistered analysis without adequate justification
issues.description: The authors deviate from their preregistered Analysis 4 by aggregating inertia and centre-of-mass understanding scores rather than analyzing them separately with 'Physical Principle' as a predictor. The stated reason is that the preregistered model 'did not converge.' However, model non-convergence is a technical issue that can be addressed through reparameterization, informative priors, or alternative estimation methods rather than by changing the outcome variable. Aggregating scores masks the theoretically important differential effects of theory type on understanding of each dimension, which are then only reported in exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated... and some individuals better understood inertia than centre of mass while others better understood centre of mass than inertia... As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score.

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses presented without appropriate labeling
issues.description: The analyses of theory type effects on exploration behavior and differential understanding (Figure 3, the core of the paper's third finding) are described as 'exploratory analyses.' However, these results are prominently featured in the abstract and discussion as key findings. The exploratory nature of these analyses is insufficiently emphasized throughout the paper, and no correction for multiple comparisons is applied. The confirmatory/exploratory distinction is blurred in a way that inflates the apparent evidential weight of these findings.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants' exploration behavior.

issues.description: In Analysis 1, data were restricted to participants' last two trials to 'limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend,' while in Analysis 3, non-descending wheels were assigned a speed of 0. These two analyses use different strategies for handling the same type of missing/censored data, which is inconsistent and could bias results differently across analyses. Assigning speed=0 to non-descending wheels is particularly problematic as it is an arbitrary value that conflates failure to descend with very slow descent, and may distort the distribution of the outcome variable.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants' last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset... Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0.

issues.subcategory: chain structure confounds individual and social learning
issues.description: Participants receive the last two configurations of the previous participant, not a random sample of configurations. This means later-generation participants inherit configurations that are already optimized, making it impossible to disentangle whether performance improvements result from social learning (copying good solutions) versus individual trial-and-error building on a better starting point. The design does not include a condition where participants start from scratch each generation, which would be necessary to isolate the effect of cultural transmission.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.description: Each participant had only 5 trials to optimize the wheel, with only the last 2 transmitted. This severely limits individual exploration and learning. With 20,736 possible configurations and only 5 trials, participants cannot systematically explore the space. The very limited number of trials may artificially suppress individual understanding (since understanding requires observing variation in outcomes) and may not be representative of real-world technological learning contexts. The constraint also means that the 'understanding' measure is taken after very limited experience.
issues.quote: Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track.

issues.description: Theories were limited to 340 characters, which may artificially constrain the quality and completeness of transmitted causal models. A full theory of the wheel dynamics requires explaining two independent physical principles, which may be difficult to convey accurately in 340 characters. This design choice may have artificially reduced the effectiveness of theory transmission, biasing results toward the null hypothesis that theory transmission has no effect.
issues.quote: Theories had to be less than 340 characters long and always started with 'The wheel covers the distance faster when...'

issues.description: The experiment uses chains of 5 individuals with only 5 trials each, which is a highly compressed simulation of cultural evolution. Real cultural transmission occurs over many more generations with much more individual experience. The authors acknowledge this is a 'conservative test' but do not adequately discuss how the artificial constraints of the laboratory setting (short chains, few trials, character-limited theories, single-session exposure) limit generalizability to real-world cumulative cultural evolution.
issues.quote: Participants were organized into chains of 5 individuals. Each participant had 5 trials to minimize the time it took for the wheel to reach the end of the track.

issues.description: The understanding test presents static images of wheel configurations and asks participants to predict which descends faster. This tests declarative/explicit knowledge but may not capture implicit procedural knowledge that guides effective exploration. A participant could improve wheel performance through implicit learning without being able to verbalize or recognize the relevant principles in a forced-choice test. The measure may therefore underestimate participants' functional understanding, which is central to the paper's main claim.
issues.quote: Participants' understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.

issues.description: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order. No counterbalancing of test item order was performed. This means order effects (e.g., fatigue, learning from earlier items) could systematically bias understanding scores in the same direction for all participants, and any item-specific difficulty effects are confounded with order position.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.description: Understanding scores are bounded (based on 10 binary forced-choice items, scores range from 0-10 or similar), yet linear models are used. A linear model can predict values outside the possible range and assumes homoscedasticity, which is unlikely for bounded outcomes. A binomial or beta-binomial model would be more appropriate. Similarly, speed data may have a non-normal distribution (especially with zeros for non-descending wheels), yet linear models are applied.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with 'Score' as the outcome variable, 'Generation' as a predictor variable and 'Chain's identity' as a random effect.

issues.subcategory: incomplete reporting of Bayesian model diagnostics
issues.description: The authors use Bayesian multilevel models fitted with map2stan but do not report standard Bayesian diagnostics such as R-hat values, effective sample sizes, trace plots, or posterior predictive checks. Without these diagnostics, it is impossible to assess whether the MCMC chains converged (beyond the one case of non-convergence mentioned) and whether the models adequately fit the data.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: The authors use Bayesian models but do not report the prior distributions used for any parameters. In Bayesian analysis, priors are a fundamental part of the model specification and affect posterior estimates, especially with small samples. The absence of prior specification makes the analyses non-reproducible and prevents assessment of whether priors were appropriate or inadvertently informative.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package.

issues.subcategory: subgroup analysis with very small N
issues.description: The exploratory analysis of theory type effects compares subgroups with very small sample sizes: 15 participants inherited an inertia theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass theory, 6 inherited a full theory, and 18 inherited irrelevant theories. The group of 6 participants who inherited a full theory is particularly small, making any conclusions about this group highly unreliable. The authors present heat maps and understanding scores for these groups without reporting uncertainty estimates appropriate for such small samples.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory... 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.description: Participants within a chain are not independent—each participant's starting point is determined by the previous participant's output. While the authors include chain identity as a random effect, the sequential dependency within chains (where each generation's performance is directly constrained by the previous generation's transmitted configurations) creates a form of autocorrelation that may not be fully captured by a simple random intercept for chain. This could affect the validity of the generation effect estimates.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain.

issues.subcategory: confound between theory content and theory quality
issues.description: The theory coding scheme classifies theories as inertia-related, centre-of-mass-related, both, or neither, but does not distinguish between accurate and inaccurate theories within each category. A theory could mention inertia but describe it incorrectly. The authors acknowledge that 'most participants actually produced incorrect or incomplete theories' but the coding scheme used for the main exploratory analyses does not capture accuracy gradations, potentially conflating the effects of theory content with theory accuracy.
issues.quote: 3 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel... and were asked to code participants' theories according to whether they contain accurate information related to moment of inertia and/or centre of mass.

issues.description: Wheel performance is measured as average speed (1m/descent time), but the payoff function used in the experiment is based on a different formula involving MaxSpeed and MinSpeed constants. The relationship between the speed metric used in analyses and the incentive structure experienced by participants is not straightforward. Additionally, using speed (a ratio) rather than time (the directly measured variable) introduces a non-linear transformation that could affect the distributional assumptions of the linear models.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations

issues.description: Participants' payoffs depend both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain. This creates a complex incentive structure where participants may strategically choose which configurations to transmit (not necessarily their best-performing ones) to maximize their own payoff. The authors state participants were informed their last two trials would be transmitted, but the interaction between this constraint and the payoff structure is not fully analyzed. Final participants had their last two payoffs doubled, creating a different incentive structure for them.
issues.quote: Participants were informed that their last two trials would be transmitted to the next participant in the chain, and that their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain.

issues.description: The authors claim '71% optimization after only four cultural generations' but the calculation basis is not clearly explained in the main text. The maximum possible speed is stated as 'about 154 m/h' but the payoff formula uses MaxSpeed=160. The discrepancy between these values and the basis for the 71% figure (what counts as 0% and 100% optimization) is not transparently reported.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.description: The sample consists exclusively of French university students, which the authors themselves acknowledge as a WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) population. The authors call for future cross-cultural work but present their conclusions about 'culturally evolving technology' and the cultural niche hypothesis in broad, universal terms. The specific physics intuitions and exploration strategies observed may be culturally specific, limiting the generalizability of the findings to the broader claims about human cultural evolution.
issues.quote: Future cross-cultural work involving non WEIRD participants should tell us whether this selective exploration is culturally constructed or shared across populations.

issues.description: The study lacks a condition where participants optimize the wheel individually across multiple sessions (equivalent to the total number of trials across a chain) without any social transmission. Without this baseline, it is impossible to determine how much of the performance improvement across generations is due to cultural transmission per se versus what a single individual could achieve with equivalent total experience. This control is essential for the paper's central claim about the role of cultural transmission.
issues.quote: To test the hypothesis that the selective retention of beneficial changes over generations can produce cultural adaptations without individual understanding, we asked successive 'cultural generations' of participants to optimize a physical system.

issues.subcategory: experimenter demand effects and lack of blinding
issues.description: The experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel based on participants' computer inputs and was present during the experiment. The authors explicitly state that 'data collection was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.' This creates potential for experimenter demand effects, particularly in the theory-writing condition where the experimenter could inadvertently signal expectations. The lack of blinding is a significant methodological limitation that is acknowledged but not adequately addressed.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: credible intervals used as hypothesis tests
issues.description: Throughout the paper, 95% credible intervals are used as the sole basis for inference, with intervals excluding zero interpreted as evidence for an effect and intervals including zero interpreted as evidence for no effect. This approach does not account for the magnitude of effects relative to practically meaningful thresholds, and the use of 95% as a threshold is arbitrary. The Bayesian framework used would allow for more principled inference via Bayes factors or posterior probabilities, which are not reported.
issues.quote: 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.description: The paper inconsistently uses 95% Confidence Intervals and 95% Highest Posterior Density Intervals (HPDI) to report uncertainty. For generation effects, CIs are reported; for mean performance values, HPDIs are reported. This inconsistency is confusing and suggests the two types of intervals may have been computed from different models or procedures. The distinction between frequentist CIs and Bayesian HPDIs is not explained.
issues.quote: Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02)... The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.description: The paper conflates several distinct types of causal understanding: explicit declarative knowledge (measured by the test), implicit procedural knowledge (reflected in exploration behavior), and the ability to generate accurate verbal theories. The conclusion that 'causal understanding is not necessary' is based on the declarative knowledge measure, but participants clearly have some functional causal knowledge (they explore the parameter space non-randomly and improve performance). The paper does not adequately distinguish these forms of understanding, which undermines the strength of the main conclusion.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that despite exhibiting poor understanding of the experimental physical system, participants did not randomly explore the parameter space.

issues.subcategory: overgeneralization from simple to complex systems
issues.description: The authors use a 2-dimensional optimization problem as a 'conservative test' and then generalize conclusions to complex multi-dimensional technologies like bows and kayaks. However, the dynamics of cultural evolution may be qualitatively different in higher-dimensional spaces where random exploration is far less efficient. The paper acknowledges this briefly but the abstract and conclusions make broad claims that are not warranted by a 2-dimensional laboratory task.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: theory transmission confounded with additional information
issues.description: In the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment, participants receive both configurations AND a theory, while in the 'Configurations' treatment they receive only configurations. Any difference between treatments could be due to the additional cognitive load of reading and processing a theory, the specific content of the theory, or the mere presence of additional text (demand characteristics). There is no condition where participants receive a neutral/irrelevant text to control for the non-specific effects of receiving additional written information.
issues.quote: In the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant's theory about the physical system.

issues.subcategory: missing descriptive statistics for theory content
issues.description: The paper reports the distribution of inherited theory types (15 inertia, 17 centre-of-mass, 6 full, 18 irrelevant) but does not report the distribution of theories produced by first-generation participants or the full distribution of theories produced across all generations. This makes it impossible to assess how theory quality evolved across generations or whether the theories transmitted were representative of those produced.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the 'Configurations + Theory' treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.description: The exploratory analyses compare multiple subgroups (4 theory types) on multiple outcomes (inertia understanding, centre-of-mass understanding, exploration patterns) without any correction for multiple comparisons. Given that these are exploratory analyses with small subgroup sizes, the probability of false positives is elevated. The authors present these results as 'striking differences' without acknowledging the inflated Type I error rate.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants' exploration behavior.

issues.description: It appears that a single experimenter (M.D.) conducted all experimental sessions, as the methods describe a single experimental room and the acknowledgments thank others only for organizing sessions. A single experimenter who is also the lead author and knows the hypotheses introduces potential for subtle experimenter effects across conditions, particularly since the experimenter physically positioned the weights on the wheel for each trial.
issues.quote: Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly.

issues.description: Figure 1 caption describes panels A-B as illustrating moment of inertia and C-D as illustrating centre of mass, but the main text describes A-D as all being part of the physical system illustration, then separately describes A-B and C-D. The figure caption also states 'A-B) The moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed around the axis' but the main text labels these as 'Figure 1.A-D' for the physical system. This inconsistency in panel labeling could confuse readers.
issues.quote: Figure 1 | Experimental task and design. A) Illustration of the physical system used in the experiment... A-B) The moment of inertia depends on how mass is distributed around the axis.

issues.subcategory: test incentive may not elicit best performance
issues.description: The understanding test offered a 5€ bonus for one randomly selected correct answer. This incentive structure (random selection of one answer) may not motivate participants to carefully consider all 10 questions, as the expected value of effort on any single question is low. A stronger incentive structure (e.g., payment for all correct answers) might have elicited more accurate measures of understanding.
issues.quote: They were also told that one of their answers will be randomly selected at the end of the test and that 5 euros will be added to their gain if that answer is correct.

issues.description: Causal understanding is measured only after participants complete all 5 trials. This means there is no baseline measure of understanding before the task, making it impossible to assess whether understanding changed as a result of participants' own experience with the wheel. The claim that understanding does not improve across generations is based on cross-sectional comparisons between generations, not within-person change, which is a weaker test of the hypothesis.
issues.quote: Participants' understanding was evaluated by presenting them with pairs of wheels that differed in their configurations, and asking them to estimate how long each wheel would take to reach the bottom of the rails.
